questions.question: What is the most appropriate first priority when AF is suspected?
choices: Assess hemodynamic stability and acute complications
Calculate long-term stroke risk before checking vital signs
Start a chronic medication without rhythm documentation
Assume all AF is asymptomatic
questions.explanation: Hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest discomfort, pulmonary edema, shock, syncope with instability, or severe respiratory distress require emergency evaluation before outpatient planning.

questions.question: Which finding can suggest atrial fibrillation but still requires rhythm confirmation?
choices: An irregularly irregular pulse
A normal temperature
One isolated cough
A stable weight
questions.explanation: An irregularly irregular pulse is a clinical clue. ECG or appropriate rhythm documentation is needed to confirm and characterize AF.

questions.question: Why are rate/rhythm management and stroke prevention separate AF decisions?
choices: Symptom or rhythm improvement does not automatically remove thromboembolic risk
All patients with AF have identical stroke risk
Rate control alone prevents every embolic event
Stroke prevention is unrelated to AF
questions.explanation: AF management addresses stability, symptoms/rate or rhythm, and thromboembolic risk separately. A patient may feel better yet still need ongoing risk assessment.

questions.question: What is the basic mechanism of embolic stroke risk in AF?
choices: Ineffective atrial contraction promotes stasis and thrombus formation that can embolize
AF always lowers blood viscosity
The ventricles stop contracting in every case
AF prevents platelet activation
questions.explanation: Disorganized atrial activity can cause blood stasis, especially in the left atrial appendage, enabling thrombus formation and systemic embolism.

questions.question: How should bleeding-risk assessment be used when considering anticoagulation?
choices: Identify and modify bleeding risks while supporting individualized risk-benefit decisions
Automatically exclude every patient with any bleeding risk
Replace thromboembolic-risk assessment
Ignore renal function and drug interactions
questions.explanation: Bleeding review helps identify factors such as NSAIDs, anemia, kidney disease, alcohol, interactions, adherence, and dose issues. It is not an automatic reason to withhold beneficial treatment.

questions.question: Which AF context requires particular anticoagulation and specialist consideration?
choices: Mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis
A normal ECG after a resolved viral cough
A patient who likes exercise
No history of any cardiovascular disease
questions.explanation: Mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis have special anticoagulation considerations and require current-guideline and specialist-informed care.

questions.question: Which is an important trigger or substrate to assess in new AF?
choices: Heart failure, hypertension, thyroid disease, infection, pulmonary disease, alcohol, stimulants, sleep apnea, and electrolyte disturbance
Only a normal office blood-pressure reading
Only a remote cholesterol test
No comorbidities matter
questions.explanation: AF often occurs with modifiable or acute contributors. Identifying them improves immediate safety and long-term recurrence prevention.

questions.question: Why does duration or uncertain onset of AF matter?
choices: It can change cardioversion and anticoagulation planning and requires current-guideline review
It never affects management
It proves the patient is stable
It eliminates the need for ECG
questions.explanation: Duration and onset uncertainty influence cardioversion safety and thromboembolic planning. Do not improvise these decisions without appropriate evaluation and collaboration.

questions.question: A patient with AF stops anticoagulation whenever bruising occurs and uses ibuprofen daily. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Assess current bleeding, dose, kidney function, interactions, anemia symptoms, access, and understanding; then coordinate a safe plan
Tell the patient bruising always means there is no stroke risk
Accept intermittent self-dosing without discussion
Ignore NSAID exposure
questions.explanation: Medication safety requires assessment of actual use, modifiable bleeding risks, dose and renal context, and patient barriers. Intermittent self-dosing can create harm.

questions.question: Which presentation requires emergency rather than routine AF follow-up?
choices: AF with hypotension, confusion, severe dyspnea, and pulmonary edema
An asymptomatic patient with a stable outpatient ECG
A patient requesting education about home pulse checks
A scheduled medication-reconciliation visit
questions.explanation: AF with instability or acute heart-failure, ischemic, respiratory, or perfusion findings requires emergency assessment and stabilization.
